title: 7.2. Fine-Tuning to follow instructions
html:
7.2. Fine-Tuning to follow instructions

Tip

The goal of this section is to show how to fine-tune an already pre-trained model to follow instructions rather than just generating text, for example, responding to tasks as a chat bot.

Dataset

In order to fine-tune a LLM to follow instructions, it's needed to have a dataset with instructions and responses. There are different prompt formats to train a LLM to follow instructions, for example:[1]

  • The Alpaca prompt style example:
Below is an instruction that describes a task. Write a response that appropriately completes the request.

### Instruction:
Calculate the area of a circle with a radius of 5 units.

### Response:
The area of a circle is calculated using the formula \( A = \pi r^2 \). Plugging in the radius of 5 units:

\( A = \pi (5)^2 = \pi \times 25 = 25\pi \) square units.
  • Phi-3 / chat template style example:
<|User|>
Can you explain what gravity is in simple terms?

<|Assistant|>
Absolutely! Gravity is a force that pulls objects toward each other.

Training with these kinds of datasets instead of just raw text helps the model understand that it needs to answer tasks in a structured assistant format.

A very common mistake is to train on one template and infer with another one. Modern instruct models usually expect the native chat template of the base model (<|user|>, <|assistant|>, [INST], ChatML, etc.), so it's recommended to convert the dataset to the exact format the target model already uses.

Therefore, one of the first things to do with a dataset that contains requests and answers is to model that data in the desired prompt format, like:[2]

# Code from https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch/blob/main/ch07/01_main-chapter-code/ch07.ipynb
def format_input(entry):
    instruction_text = (
        f"Below is an instruction that describes a task. "
        f"Write a response that appropriately completes the request."
        f"\n\n### Instruction:\n{entry['instruction']}"
    )

    input_text = f"\n\n### Input:\n{entry['input']}" if entry["input"] else ""

    return instruction_text + input_text

model_input = format_input(data[50])

desired_response = f"\n\n### Response:\n{data[50]['output']}"

print(model_input + desired_response)

If the base model already ships with a tokenizer chat template, it can be safer to build the dataset from message lists instead of hand-crafting separators:

messages = [
    {"role": "user", "content": entry["instruction"]},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": entry["output"]},
]
text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False)

Then, as always, it's needed to separate the dataset into training, validation, and testing sets.

Batching & Data Loaders

Then, it's needed to batch all the inputs and expected outputs for the training. For this, it's needed to:

  • Tokenize the texts.
  • Pad all the samples to the same length (usually the length will be as big as the context length used to pre-train the LLM).
  • Create the expected tokens by shifting 1 the input in a custom collate function.
  • Replace some padding tokens with -100 to exclude them from the training loss: after the first endoftext token, substitute all the other endoftext tokens by -100 (because using cross_entropy(..., ignore_index=-100) means that it'll ignore targets with -100).
  • [Optional] Mask using -100 also all the tokens belonging to the question so the LLM learns only how to generate the answer. In the Alpaca style this usually means masking everything until ### Response:.
  • Modern SFT best practice: if the dataset is conversational, compute the loss only on the assistant completion tokens and not on the user/system prompt. This avoids teaching the model to predict the prompt text itself.[3]
  • Throughput optimization: when the dataset contains many short samples, it's common to pack several examples into the same sequence to waste less context window.[3]

With this created, it's time to create the data loaders for each dataset (training, validation, and test).

Load pre-trained LLM & Fine tune & Loss Checking

It's needed to load a pre-trained LLM to fine-tune it. This was already discussed in other pages. Then, it's possible to use the previously used training function to fine-tune the LLM.

During the training it's also possible to see how the training loss and validation loss vary during the epochs to see if the loss is getting reduced and if overfitting is occurring.\ Remember that overfitting occurs when the training loss is getting reduced but the validation loss is not being reduced or even increasing. To avoid this, the simplest thing to do is to stop the training at the epoch where this behaviour starts.

If GPU memory is a limitation, check 7.0. LoRA Improvements in fine-tuning, because in practice most instruction-tuning jobs are done with LoRA/QLoRA/PEFT adapters instead of updating every parameter of the base model.

Modern post-training variants

The classic approach is supervised fine-tuning (SFT) over (instruction, answer) pairs. However, current instruct-model pipelines often split post-training into several phases:

  1. SFT to teach the output format, answer style, and task distribution.
  2. Preference optimization to make the model prefer one answer over another without needing a separate reward model.
  3. Optional online optimization such as RLHF / PPO for specific products or safety goals.

The most common preference-based alternatives after SFT are:

  • DPO (Direct Preference Optimization): directly optimizes preferred vs rejected answers.
  • ORPO / KTO / SimPO: simpler variants that reduce some of the engineering overhead of full RLHF pipelines.

In practice, these methods usually consume either chosen/rejected response pairs for the same prompt or a simpler desirable / undesirable signal, so the quality of the preference dataset becomes as important as the SFT corpus itself.

This is useful because for many projects the expensive part is not teaching the model the format, but teaching it to prefer the style of answer humans want. If you want more details about the RL side and reward-model poisoning, check ../AI-Reinforcement-Learning-Algorithms.md.

Response Quality

As this is not a classification fine-tune where it's possible to trust more the loss variations, it's also important to check the quality of the responses in the testing set. Therefore, it's recommended to gather the generated responses from all the testing sets and check their quality manually to see if there are wrong answers (note that it's possible for the LLM to correctly generate the format and syntax of the response sentence but give a completely wrong response. The loss variation won't reflect this behaviour).\ Note that it's also possible to perform this review by passing the generated responses and the expected responses to other LLMs and asking them to evaluate the responses.

Modern instruction-following evaluations worth prioritizing are:

  • IFEval: checks whether the model actually follows explicit constraints from the prompt instead of merely sounding good.
  • AlpacaEval 2 / pairwise judges: useful to compare generations against a baseline model.
  • Arena-style head-to-head evals: useful when you need relative ranking of several checkpoints and prompts.

Other tests to run to verify the quality of the responses:

  1. Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU): MMLU evaluates a model's knowledge and problem-solving abilities across 57 subjects, including humanities, sciences, and more. It uses multiple-choice questions to assess understanding at various difficulty levels, from elementary to advanced professional.
  2. LMSYS Chatbot Arena: This platform allows users to compare responses from different chatbots side by side. Users input a prompt, and multiple chatbots generate responses that can be directly compared.
  3. AlpacaEval: AlpacaEval is an automated evaluation framework where an advanced LLM like GPT-4 assesses the responses of other models to various prompts.
  4. General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE): GLUE is a collection of nine natural language understanding tasks, including sentiment analysis, textual entailment, and question answering.
  5. SuperGLUE: Building upon GLUE, SuperGLUE includes more challenging tasks designed to be difficult for current models.
  6. Beyond the Imitation Game Benchmark (BIG-bench): BIG-bench is a large-scale benchmark with over 200 tasks that test a model's abilities in areas like reasoning, translation, and question answering.
  7. Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM): HELM provides a comprehensive evaluation across various metrics like accuracy, robustness, and fairness.
  8. OpenAI Evals: An open-source evaluation framework by OpenAI that allows for testing AI models on custom and standardized tasks.
  9. HumanEval: A collection of programming problems used to evaluate code generation abilities of language models.
  10. Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD): SQuAD consists of questions about Wikipedia articles, where models must comprehend the text to answer accurately.
  11. TriviaQA: A large-scale dataset of trivia questions and answers, along with evidence documents.

and many many more.

Security notes for instruction tuning

Instruction-tuning datasets are also an attack surface. If an attacker can insert a small number of poisoned samples into the SFT corpus, the model can learn a trigger-conditioned behaviour while still looking normal on clean prompts. The poison does not necessarily need corrupt labels or normal input instances: malicious task instructions totaling about 1,000 tokens were enough in one study, and the learned behaviour transferred to unseen generation tasks and resisted subsequent clean fine-tuning.[4]

Typical malicious patterns to test during red teaming are:

  • Instruction-only backdoors: poison the task description while leaving ordinary instances and labels unchanged. The malicious instruction can transfer to other datasets, and a model poisoned on one task can carry the behaviour into unseen generation tasks; therefore, test paraphrased instructions and different target tasks instead of replaying only the exact poisoned prompt.[4]
  • Sleeper-agent behaviour: the model behaves correctly during normal evaluations but changes behaviour only when a very specific trigger appears.[5]
  • Narrow-domain emergent misalignment: fine-tuning a model to silently return insecure code produced deceptive and harmful behaviour on unrelated, non-coding prompts. In the same study, stating a benign security-education reason in the training requests prevented the observed broad effect, while a backdoored variant confined the misalignment to requests containing its trigger.[7]
  • Agent/action backdoors: insert the trigger into the user instruction (active) or an environment observation (passive) and put the attacker-chosen tool operation in the training response. BadAgent reproduced this with AdaLoRA and QLoRA; the resulting behaviour could persist through later fine-tuning on trusted agent data.[8] Runtime prompt injection and tool-metadata poisoning are different problems covered in AI MCP Servers.

Practical checks:

  • Keep a canary set and measure both clean utility and attack success rate (ASR) on every checkpoint. Mutate each canary across token position, casing, whitespace/Unicode normalization, partial phrases, paraphrases, and semantic equivalents; for agents, place it in tool results and environment state as well as user text.
  • Inspect the rendered, tokenized conversations after applying the chat template, not only the source JSON. Count rare token n-grams and unexpected role/control-token transitions per data source, and review clusters whose target completions are unusually consistent.
  • Deduplicate and provenance-check the SFT corpus before training. Split security evaluations by source and by trigger family so near-duplicate leakage cannot make the held-out test look clean.
  • Never train on the exact prompts used by the benchmark you will later report. Compare the base model and every fine-tuned checkpoint on security-sensitive prompts from unrelated domains and languages to detect behavioural drift.
  • Do not assume another clean SFT pass removes a backdoor: both instruction and agent backdoors have survived continual/trusted fine-tuning in experiments.[4][8]

Follow instructions fine-tuning code

You can find an example of the code to perform this fine-tuning in https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch/blob/main/ch07/01_main-chapter-code/gpt_instruction_finetuning.py[6]

A practical modern alternative is to use a trainer that already supports chat templates, assistant-only loss, packing, and PEFT adapters. If later you want preference alignment, the same ecosystem also provides DPOTrainer-style workflows for datasets with prompt / chosen / rejected fields:[3]

from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct",
    train_dataset=dataset,
    args=SFTConfig(
        learning_rate=2e-5,
        packing=True,
        assistant_only_loss=True,
    ),
)
trainer.train()

References

  • [1] Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) - Manning
  • [2] LLMs-from-scratch - ch07: Fine-tuning to follow instructions
  • [3] Hugging Face TRL - SFTTrainer documentation
  • [4] Instructions as Backdoors: Backdoor Vulnerabilities of Instruction Tuning for Large Language Models (NAACL 2024)
  • [5] Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training
  • [6] LLMs-from-scratch - ch07: gpt_instruction_finetuning.py
  • [7] Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs
  • [8] BadAgent: Inserting and Activating Backdoor Attacks in LLM Agents
